people.name: Alberto Fujimori
people.summary: President of Peru, 1990-2000. Prosecutors accused him as an indirect perpetrator (autor mediato) of the 1990s sterilisation programme: grave injury followed by death of five women and grave injury to about 1,300. A judge opened proceedings in December 2021, with his part suspended pending Chile's view on his extradition; the courts later annulled them. He was never tried on this and died in September 2024. Prosecutors archived the file in October 2026 as time-barred; the victims' lawyers say they will seek review.

records.what: Prosecutor Marcelita Gutiérrez filed a formal complaint naming him as an indirect perpetrator (RPP, 12 November 2018).

At a hearing on Monday 1 March 2021, prosecutor Pablo Espinoza said the then executive built "todo un marco jurídico para evitar ser responsables", and that health staff were coerced to meet sterilisation targets and received incentives (CNN Chile). The prosecutor said the former president had a majority in Congress and "pudo modificar las leyes para legalizar la esterilización".

On 11 December 2021 Judge Rafael Martínez opened criminal proceedings, for grave injury followed by death in a context of grave human rights violation; Fujimori's part was suspended pending Chile's view on extending his extradition.
The courts confirmed annulment of the accusation in August, which voided proceedings from 2021 to 2023 and returned the case to the prosecutor's stage. He died that September (El Tiempo).

Archived: Peru's Fourth Supranational Human Rights Prosecutor's Office closed the file by Disposición Fiscal 25, dated 22 October 2026 (teleSUR), as time-barred under a 2024 law, Ley 32107, that bars treating acts before July 2002 as crimes against humanity; criminal action was extinguished for 52 people (teleSUR; AFP in Diário de Notícias). Sigfredo Florián of the Instituto de Defensa Legal said the victims' defence will appeal to a senior human rights prosecutor (El Búho); Rocío Silva-Santisteban of Demus told AFP a complaint will go to a higher prosecutor. No result had been reported on the pages opened, the latest dated 30 October 2026. The pages opened list the former ministers among the 52 and do not say whether he is one of them; he had died two years earlier.

people.name: Marino Costa Bauer

They accused him as an indirect perpetrator; a senior prosecutor had ordered him tried as co-author of grave injury. A judge opened proceedings in December 2021, which were later annulled. Never tried or convicted. The file was archived in October 2026 as time-barred; the victims' lawyers say they will seek review.

people.name: Tika Ram Adhikari
people.summary: Chief warden of Chitwan National Park in 2006, when Shikharam Chaudhary died after detention by park staff. He told investigators he approved a 15-day investigation; he told the Kathmandu Post he saw the man only once. Suspended by the ministry and charged with homicide with two others; the district court ordered them held on remand. Nepal's Cabinet dismissed the case on 4 March 2007, so there was no verdict. He later became director general of the national parks department. He says the death was caused by illness.

posts.org: Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, Nepal

records.what: The forest ministry suspended him, Kamal Jung Kunwar and ranger Ritesh Basnet as they were taken into police custody, on a complaint by the dead man's brother (The Himalayan Times, 14 June 2006).

After homicide charges and a rejected appeal to the Hetauda Appellate Court, the Cabinet under Girija Prasad Koirala decided on 4 March 2007 to dismiss the case. WWF Nepal's press release welcomed this.

sources.title: Asia News Network (Kathmandu Post): Nepali park officials tortured a man to death

people.disputed: Charged, not convicted: the case was dismissed by Cabinet decision, not by a court. His reply: "He was mentally ill. His death was caused by his illness." He told the Post he knew of no torture. Activist Chabilal Neupane told the Post the warden had been told of the man's worsening health days before the death and said: "it was necessary to put pressure on detainees during the investigation process". The Himalayan Times calls him chief of the park.

people.summary: Commander of the Libyan coast guard unit at Zawiya. The UN Security Council sanctioned him in 2018, citing its Panel of Experts that he was directly involved in sinking migrant boats with firearms. Arrested in Tripoli in about October 2020; Tripoli's military attorney general dropped the charges for lack of evidence in April 2021. Never convicted on the pages opened. Killed on 1 September 2024.

people.name: Osama Elmasry Njeem
people.summary: Alleged to have run prison facilities in Tripoli including Mitiga. The ICC issued a warrant on 18 January 2025 for war crimes and crimes against humanity from February 2015, including murder, torture and rape of detainees; the warrant stands and he has not been tried there. New Lines says he led judicial police that intercepted migrants at sea. Arrested in Turin and flown back to Libya within days. Convicted in Tripoli: the attorney general's office announced on 21 June 2026 a sentence of 7 years 4 months for violating detainees' rights. That is a lesser and narrower case than the ICC's. Whether he is held is disputed.

posts.role: Alleged by the ICC to be in charge of prison facilities

records.what: ICC warrant issued 18 January; arrested in Turin on 19 January; released and returned to Libya on 21 January "without prior notice or consultation with the Court".
Libya's attorney general said he was in pretrial detention, questioned over abuses against ten inmates including one death under torture (Reuters, 5 November).

Tripoli Criminal Court: 7 years 4 months, and loss of legal capacity and civil rights for the term plus a year, for violating the rights of inmates who reported "torture, cruelty and degrading treatment" (AP via WTOP, 21 June). Il Post says the case concerned ten migrants, one of whom died.

HRW, 16 July: the ICC prosecutor's office has no confirmation of the detention from Libya, and "other sources have indicated that Njeem is not currently detained". The warrant alleges at least 34 killings; the Libyan case reportedly covered 10 detainees and one death.

people.name: Paolo Gentiloni
people.summary: As Italy's prime minister he signed the Italy-Libya migration memorandum in Rome on 2 February 2017. The memorandum committed Italy to "technical and technological support to Libyan bodies in charge of the fight against illegal immigration", which Il Sole 24 Ore says include the border and coast guard under Libya's defence ministry, and to funding what it calls temporary reception centres under the "exclusive control" of Libya's interior ministry (EU Migration Law Blog). A UN investigator said in 2023 that EU and member state support has aided and abetted crimes in Libya, while saying they did not commit them. No court or prosecutor has made a finding against him on any page opened.

records.what: Signed the memorandum with Fayez al-Serraj in Rome on 2 February.

UN investigator Chaloka Beyani: "We're not saying that the EU and its member states have committed these crimes", but "the support given has aided and abetted the commission of the crimes". He named no individual on the page opened.

people.name: Fayez al-Serraj
people.summary: Head of Libya's UN-backed Government of National Accord. He signed the migration memorandum with Italy in Rome on 2 February 2017. The memorandum committed Italy to "technical and technological support to Libyan bodies in charge of the fight against illegal immigration", which Il Sole 24 Ore says include the border and coast guard under Libya's defence ministry, and to funding what it calls temporary reception centres under the "exclusive control" of Libya's interior ministry (EU Migration Law Blog). Those are bodies of the government he headed. No court or prosecutor has made a finding against him on any page opened, and no page shows he commanded them.

After the Tripoli Court of Appeal suspended the memorandum, his government's justice ministry said on 23 March it was "never meant to include the return of migrants from Italy to new EU-funded camps in Libya" (Libya Herald). The Supreme Court later reversed the suspension for lack of jurisdiction (EU Migration Law Blog).

people.name: John C. Cutler
people.summary: US Public Health Service doctor who led the 1946-1948 experiments in Guatemala, deliberately exposing about 1,300 prisoners, soldiers, psychiatric patients and sex workers to syphilis, gonorrhoea or chancroid, with NIH grant money. A US presidential commission said in 2011 of him and the other researchers: 'Their failure to exercise moral leadership cannot be excused.' A commission is not a court; no charge on any page opened. He died in 2003.

records.what: Led the study with Juan Funes of Guatemala's venereal disease division, who offered the study population (Hektoen). Records show 1,308 subjects and 83 deaths during the experiments, causes poorly documented (Clinician).
Died; an obituary was published on 12 February 2003 (Indian Journal of Medical Ethics, which gives no exact date).
The commission called the practices "heinous" and wrote: "They thought that they were above the rules."

people.disputed: Criticised by a presidential commission; no charge or conviction on any page opened. Cutler stated that all participants received treatment; Hektoen says the treatment records are incomplete. people.name: Théoneste Bagosora
people.summary: Director of cabinet at Rwanda's defence ministry in 1994, convicted by the UN Rwanda tribunal of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In the BNP case, complainants and Open Secrets say he went to the Seychelles in June 1994 to buy arms from Willem Ehlers, and that $1.3 million moved from the Rwandan central bank's BNP account to Ehlers. That payment is alleged, and no court has ruled on it. He died in 2021.

records.what: Alleged, not found by any court. Open Secrets, whose account follows the 2017 complaint: after traveller's cheques failed, he contacted Joseph Nzirorera, who asked the central bank governor to pay. Transfers it lists to Ehlers's Swiss account from the central bank's BNP account: $592,784 on 14 June and $734,099 on 16 June. Sources told it the investigation shows only that the matter merits inquiry, not guilt.
The tribunal sentenced him to life on 18 December 2008; on appeal on 14 December 2011 the term was cut to 35 years (TRIAL International in Global Voices; Africanews).
Died in a hospital in Mali, aged 80, serving his sentence; reported 27 September 2021 as having died on the Saturday (25 September).

sources.title: Unaccountable / Open Secrets, BNP Paribas (4 December 2024)

people.disputed: Convicted at the tribunal for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes; that conviction does not cover the BNP transfer, which is alleged by NGOs in a French complaint under investigation since 2017, with no ruling. BNP did not respond to Open Secrets. The appeals chamber did not find he ordered the crimes, but found he knew of them and did nothing to prevent them despite having the means (Africanews). He always denied his alleged role. At the tribunal he confirmed that weapons from the Seychelles via Goma were to "give a hand to Kigali" (Global Voices).
anchor: Kigali, seat of the Rwandan defence ministry in 1994 (city level)
people.placed_basis: Defence ministry post, Kigali.

people.name: Georges Chodron de Courcel
people.summary: Group chief operating officer of BNP Paribas. New York's banking regulator says that at a September 2005 meeting, called by Geneva compliance officers over transactions for Sudanese customers, he dismissed their concerns and asked that no minutes be taken. The regulator lists him among 13 people who left the bank as a result of its investigation. Not personally charged on any page opened. BNP pleaded guilty as a company. The bank said in 2014 that he stepped down at his own request.

BNP announced on 12 June that he would stand down on 30 June "at his own request" and retire on 30 September, citing a new French banking law on directorships. AFP's anonymous sources said New York regulator Benjamin Lawsky pressed for his departure.
DFS: "13 individuals were terminated by or separated from the Bank as a result of the investigation"; he is named among them.

people.name: Herminio Disini
people.summary: Associate of Ferdinand Marcos who, the Supreme Court found, acted as Special Sales Representative for Westinghouse and Burns & Roe on the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant. The Court held on 15 January 2021 that he used his closeness to Marcos to steer the contract, and ordered damages. It reduced the award in a resolution dated 29 August 2023 and made public in February 2024, which falls on his estate. Civil, not criminal. He died in June 2014.

The Court denied the Republic's motion with finality and cut temperate damages to P100 million: "No further pleadings or motions shall be entertained in this case."
